question: What makes droplet nuclei so tricky when it comes to spreading infections?

options.A: Blocking the entry of viruses into the upper respiratory tract
options.B: Causing localized skin infections through direct contact
options.C: Settling immediately on nearby surfaces within one meter
options.D: Carrying airborne infectious pathogens over long distances

explanation: Great job thinking about how germs travel! Droplet nuclei are tiny dried-out particles that stay floating in the air for a long time, letting them travel far on air currents. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h1)

question: Why can't nurses rely on regular surgical masks when caring for patients with airborne diseases?

options.A: Surgical masks trap moisture and destroy bacterial filters
options.B: Pathogens are small enough to pass through regular mask material
options.C: Droplet nuclei can easily bypass loose-fitting surgical masks
options.D: Surgical masks only protect against blood splashes

explanation: You've got this! Regular surgical masks aren't tightly sealed enough around the edges, meaning those sneaky floating droplet nuclei can slip right past them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h1)

question: Which of these bacterial airborne illnesses is still a major health concern across Nigeria?
explanation: Spot on! Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial infection that affects the lungs and remains a huge focus for public health and nursing here in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h2)

question: If a Nigerian community suddenly sees an outbreak of measles, what is the most likely cause?

options.A: Low routine immunization coverage among children
options.B: High mosquito vector breeding during the rainy season
options.C: Unsafe disposal of hospital sharp instruments

explanation: Well done! Measles is totally preventable with vaccines, so sudden outbreaks usually mean kids in the area are missing their routine shots. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h2)

question: What is a classic warning sign that a patient might have pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: Painful ulcers forming inside the oral cavity
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the sclera and skin
options.C: Sudden swelling of the lower extremities
options.D: A persistent cough lasting more than two weeks

explanation: That's right! Whenever a patient walks in with a cough that just won't quit for over two weeks, TB should immediately pop into your nursing mind. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h3)

question: A patient arrives at your clinic with a long-term cough, heavy night sweats, and sudden weight loss. What should you do first?

options.A: Placing the patient in isolation precautions
options.C: Checking the patient for peripheral edema

explanation: Safety first! Those classic signs point right to TB, so your immediate priority is protecting everyone else in the clinic by isolating the patient. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h3)

question: Why do nurses collect a sputum sample from a patient they suspect has tuberculosis?

options.A: To test for acid-fast bacilli and confirm infection
options.B: To check for elevated white blood cell counts
options.C: To determine the patient's blood electrolyte levels
options.D: To measure the exact oxygen saturation in the lungs

explanation: You're doing great! Sputum microscopy looks specifically for acid-fast bacilli, which are the telltale bacteria responsible for causing TB. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h4)

question: Why is it so important to tell a patient to cough up deep lung mucus instead of just spitting out mouth saliva for a TB test?

options.A: Deep-lung samples prevent the patient from coughing blood
options.B: Saliva damages the expensive laboratory testing equipment
options.C: Saliva does not contain the actual bacteria from the lungs
options.D: Saliva samples take much longer to process in the lab

explanation: Makes total sense, right? TB lives deep in the lungs, so mouth saliva won't show us the bacteria we need to find for an accurate diagnosis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h4)

question: What special type of room ventilation is a must-have for patients on airborne precautions?
explanation: Spot on! Negative pressure rooms act like a trap—when the door opens, air rushes in instead of letting infectious germs float out into the hospital hallway. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h5)

question: A patient with active TB needs to go for an X-ray in another part of the hospital. What must the nurse do?

options.A: Ensure the patient wears an N95 respirator mask
options.B: Have the patient wear a standard surgical mask
options.C: Transport the patient during peak visiting hours
options.D: Instruct the patient to hold their breath in hallways

explanation: You've got this! Putting a simple surgical mask on the patient catches their respiratory droplets right at the source while they are moving through the hospital. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h5)

question: In a busy clinic with limited resources, what is one of the best ways to reduce airborne germ spread?

options.A: Turning off ceiling fans to stop particle circulation
options.B: Installing expensive high-efficiency particulate air scrubbers
options.C: Sealing all clinical rooms to prevent outside air entry
options.D: Ensuring optimal natural ventilation by opening windows and doors

explanation: Simple and effective! When high-tech ventilation isn't available, opening up doors and windows lets fresh outdoor air sweep those germs away. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h6)

question: Why does quickly sorting (triage) a coughing patient help stop airborne infections in a crowded clinic?

options.A: It isolates infectious individuals away from the general waiting crowd
options.B: It eliminates the need for any staff personal protective equipment
options.C: It immediately cures the underlying respiratory infection
options.D: It guarantees that laboratory test results return within minutes

explanation: Brilliant nursing logic! Spotting coughing patients early and moving them away from other waiting patients stops germs from spreading in the waiting room. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h6)

question: What is the correct way to practice good cough etiquette to stop airborne germs from spreading?

options.A: Covering the face tightly with bare hands during a cough
options.B: Turning the head downward toward shared floor surfaces
options.C: Sputum expulsion directly into open waste bins
options.D: Covering the mouth and nose with a tissue or the inner elbow

explanation: Exactly! Using a tissue or coughing into your inner elbow keeps those germs off your hands so you don't pass them to door handles or other people. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h7)

question: Why is fighting social stigma just as important as giving medicine when dealing with airborne diseases?

options.A: Social isolation changes the physical structure of droplet nuclei
options.B: Community rumors replace the need for diagnostic laboratory tests
options.C: Fear of discrimination often causes patients to delay seeking care
options.D: Stigma directly inactivates the bacteria inside the lungs

explanation: So true! When people are afraid of being judged or stigmatized, they hide their sickness and stay away from clinics, which unfortunately lets the disease spread further. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h7)
